title: Thundering Herd
briefing: A shopping feed on launch day: 4,000 requests a second at opening, 30,000 a minute later. 99% are reads of a million items, and a few thousand popular ones get most of them. Even the smallest cache holds every item.
Warm, the cache answers almost every read and the database idles. Then, a minute and a half in, the cache node restarts. It comes back empty, and every read misses at once.

Make the database survive that moment. A cache can coalesce misses (the first miss on an item fetches it, the rest wait for that fetch), keep a replica that takes over warm, or the database can simply be big enough.
debrief: Warm, a cache with a 5-minute TTL answers about 94% of reads. A large database then sees about 1,600 reads and 300 writes a second (750 read-equivalents): 24% busy. A medium one would be 48%, which is why it's tempting.

The moment the cache comes back empty, the database gets all 29,700 reads plus the writes: 304% of a large one. The popular items come back fast, three quarters of reads hit again within a second, but only once their fetch returns, and the database's queue is now a second long. Until then every read of even the most popular item misses too, and joins the queue: the stampede. About 12,600 requests time out, nearly three times the 4,600 the run can lose.

Coalescing breaks the loop: the database sees one read per item instead of thousands, and a large database rides it out. A replicated cache never goes cold, for $30 more a month, so even a medium database copes. Or an xlarge database takes 20,000 reads a second and absorbs the burst, for $600 more. Coalescing can't rescue a database too small for the refill, though: a medium one still times out requests for ten seconds.

Facebook's Memcache hands out leases so that only one client refills a key; Go's singleflight and Varnish's request coalescing do the same, and production caches warm a replacement before it takes traffic. In an interview, whenever you add a cache, say what happens when it's empty.

solutions.name: Coalesce misses
solutions.explanation: The empty cache sends each item's first miss to the large database and holds the rest until that fetch returns. The database's queue never fills.

solutions.name: A replicated cache
solutions.explanation: When the node restarts, its replica takes over with every item still cached, so the database never notices. Doubling a $30 cache is the cheapest protection, enough even for a medium database.

solutions.name: A database big enough for the burst
solutions.explanation: An xlarge database takes 20,000 reads a second. The empty cache sends it more for a moment, but it refills too fast for the queue to fill.

antiSolutions.name: Built for the warm cache
antiSolutions.explanation: A medium database is 48% busy while the cache is warm, and 609% the moment it's empty.

antiSolutions.name: A large database, unprotected
antiSolutions.explanation: 304% of capacity when the cache empties. Refills wait in the database's queue, so for a second even the popular items keep missing, and about 12,600 requests time out.

antiSolutions.name: Coalescing in front of a medium database
antiSolutions.explanation: Coalescing stops the duplicate reads, but refilling the cache still takes more than a medium database has: it times out requests for ten seconds.

antiSolutions.name: No cache, the biggest database
antiSolutions.explanation: 29,700 reads a second is 152% of an xlarge database, all the time.
